title: Challenge: Permutation Backtracking

writing.exampleCaption: Complete std-only permutations program for its typed teaching fixture. Parsing and output construction are separate from the core algorithm.
writing.explanation:
Each position needs a distinct input item while sibling branches reuse available choices. The worked program demonstrates this invariant on an independent fixture, so you can study the implementation before predicting the challenge result.

For teaching input `[1,2,3]`, the worked program returns `6`. Its functions are complete and use only std. Adapt the same state transitions to the visible challenge input `[1,2,3,4]`; predict that result before opening the answer reveal. The precise contract is: Given [...], return the number of permutations of the distinct items, counting one empty permutation for an empty list. Given list=[...], return every permutation instead, trying unused input positions left to right, with commas within a permutation and semicolons between them.

Return canonical output: lowercase booleans, decimal integers without leading zeros, comma-separated values and semicolon-separated groups, with no extra whitespace or final newline. Whole medians use integer form and half medians use .5. Textual sentinels such as none and # retain their stated meaning. String and character-grid fixtures use ASCII unless the lesson explicitly specifies Unicode scalar values.

Solve the exact task, not just the visible example: Given [...], return the number of permutations of the distinct items, counting one empty permutation for an empty list. Given list=[...], return every permutation instead, trying unused input positions left to right, with commas within a permutation and semicolons between them. On input `[1,2,3,4]`, predict the output before opening the answer reveal. The revealed output is a test oracle for this case, while private checks exercise other legal cases. Start by stating the input grammar and output format in your own words. Parse the complete input, including surrounding whitespace, before relying on any convenient positions in the example.

Build the solution around one maintained claim: Choose one unused item for the next position, recurse, then mark it unused again. Decide what state represents that claim, how it is initialized, what a single update does, and when the algorithm stops. Most patterns here explore a decision tree; meet-in-the-middle instead enumerates two halves and combines them. Define the partial choice or subset summary that the pattern retains. Trace the visible input by hand and record at least two intermediate states, not only the final answer. If the trace cannot justify your predicted output, there is a gap between the idea and the implementation.

Check both correctness and cost. The intended bound is O(n*n!) time · O(n) state excluding output; explain which operation dominates it and how many times the input can trigger that operation. Test no solution, one solution, duplicate inputs, and the order in which candidates are tried if output order is observable. Add one small case that should succeed, one boundary case, and one case chosen to challenge the invariant. Compare your hand result with the program's result, then use a failing case to fix the earliest incorrect state transition rather than patching the final output.
writing.feedback: For this input the result is `120`. Each position needs a distinct input item while sibling branches reuse available choices. Compare this independent fixture with the worked trace: Four distinct items offer 4 choices, then 3, then 2, then 1, producing 24 leaves. Unmarking after recursion restores the parent's choice set. The function builds every permutation; the count is the length of that list.
